newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: ASIAN EXOTICS - Rupiah rises on tight liquidity.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN EXOTICS - Rupiah rises on tight liquidity.

text.p: Most regional currencies saw subdued activity on Tuesday as players were reluctant to take fresh positions ahead of the Federal Reserve's policy-making meeting later in the day.
Dealers said a 25-basis-point rate hike was widely expected but the market was nervous about the possibility of a more aggressive move by the Fed.
In Indonesia, the rupiah had an active morning, firming amid tightened liquidity as state banks held back funds in anticipation of large tax payments for the financial year end on March 31.
Jakarta dealers said higher year-end tax payments seemed to cause overnight money to soar, the dollar to fall and swap rates to rise across the board.
Spot rupiah rose to a high of 2,397.0 before settling at 2,398.50/99.50 at 0450 GMT. It opened at 2,401.0/02.0.
Overnight money soared to a high of 20.0/22.0 percent from 8.5/9.0 percent and overnight swaps to 1.0/1.2 from par/0.1 points.
Dealers said another factor keeping the market worried was the upcoming new reserve requirement rate of five percent which will be effective from April 16.
They said many operators had been covering opening short swap positions since Monday to cash out from the market as they could not anticipate the short-term liquidity outlook.
A foreign bank dealer said the possibility of a U.S. rate hike seemed to have little impact on the market.
"The focus is on liquidity. A possible hike seem to have been widely discounted," the dealer said.
"Besides, this is positive in the sense that it would narrow interest rate differentials between the two currencies to help curb recent heavy capital inflows," he added.
A Singapore-based dealer said the dollar should be supported around 2,396.00 but she would sell it on any rallies to 2,402.0/03.0.
The Singapore dollar settled into a quieter range after Monday's sharp rise, but dealers said it remained underpinned by Finance Minister Richard Hu's comments at the weekend.

Hu's remark that the Singapore dollar could be expected to maintain its more modest rise of recent years if the global inflationary environment remained favourable triggered a sell-off in dollar/Sing on Monday.
The move was sharpened by a joint statement by Singapore and Brunei categorically denying earlier market speculation that they might de-link their currencies.

"Dollar/Sing is unable to climb above 1.4400 because the market is still very long dollars. So there's a possibility it will go down to 1.4350 but I'm looking for a deeper correction to 1.4300 to pick up dollars," said a European bank dealer.
She said the overall uptrend was still intact for dollar/Sing and the Malaysian ringgit/Sing cross but Monday's events had provided the impetus for a much-needed correction.

Research firm I.D.E.A. said the prospect of yield spreads widening if the United States entered a mild tightening phase implied it was not a good time "to aggressively recommit to the Singapore dollar".
The Malaysian ringgit remained stuck within its recent range as players focused on the outcome of the Fed meeting in the absence of other leads.
"Market consensus is for a 25-point hike. Any surprises and we'll be very volatile," said a Malaysian bank dealer.
The Singapore-based dealer said dollar/ringgit was likely to remain in a 2.4755-2.4795 range.
In Thailand, the baht was easier in line with the dollar's firm tone and ample money market liquidity, which dampened short-term interest rates.
"The (baht) short-term interest rate is very low. It's better to hold the dollar than baht," said a senior dealer at a Bangkok bank.
The baht was quoted at 25.975-25.980 to the dollar at 0450 GMT against 25.961/25.964 late on Monday. The Bank of Thailand fixed the mid-rate at 25.96 per dollar compared with 25.94 on Monday.
-- Reme Ahmad in Kuala Lumpur (603-230 8911), Mantik Kusjanto in Jakarta (6221-384-6364), Anuchit Nguyen in Bangkok (662) 652-0642 and Sonali Desai in Singapore (65-8703090)
